Costco workforce planning: code appendix¶

Texas MISA Fall 2026 case competition. Simulated data: every number in this notebook comes from the case's data pack, which the organizers simulated. None of it is real Costco data.

This is the code behind our staffing plan for the week of Feb 12-18, 2026. Read top to bottom, it shows each step's code, what the code produced, and what we concluded. It reruns the whole analysis from the data pack, and the last section checks every result against the files we submitted.

How to run it. From the repository root, python scripts/build_notebook.py rebuilds this notebook, runs it and exports the HTML, which takes a few minutes. Or open deliverables/Costco_Analysis_Appendix.ipynb in Jupyter with the repository root as the working directory and run all cells. README.md has the setup steps.

How to read it. Each section opens with what it shows and ends with a takeaway. Numbers are printed by the code cells, never typed into the prose. The real functions from src/ are shown with inspect.getsource, so the code you read here is the code that made the plan. IDs point to the planning notes: F for findings (planning/FINDINGS.md), A for assumptions (ASSUMPTIONS.md), D for decisions (DECISIONS.md).

§ Section What it answers
1 The data Can we trust the data, and what is its grain?
2 Diagnosis What went wrong in history, and how would the draft schedule fare?
3 Forecast How much demand should the planning week expect, block by block?
4 Service curves How busy can a block run before it misses its service target?
5 Risk model What chance does a block have of meeting target at a given headcount?
6 Allocation and cost How is a headcount filled and costed?
7 Staffing search What headcount should each block get?
8 Trade-offs What do the service goal, the callout allowance and holiday PTO cost?
9 Scenarios How do BASE, PEAK and DISRUPT differ?
10 Submission Is the submitted file complete and valid?
11 Reproducibility Does this notebook reproduce the submitted results?

_CODE_STYLE = HtmlFormatter(noclasses=True, style="friendly", nobackground=True,
                            prestyles="font-family:Consolas,'Cascadia Mono',Menlo,monospace;font-size:12px;line-height:1.45;"
                                      "white-space:pre-wrap;margin:8px 0")


def show_code(*objects):
    """Display the real source of functions or classes from src/, with where each one lives."""
    parts, places = [], []
    for obj in objects:
        lines, start = inspect.getsourcelines(obj)
        path = Path(inspect.getsourcefile(inspect.unwrap(obj))).resolve().relative_to(ROOT).as_posix()
        places.append(f"<code>{path}</code> line {start}: <b>{obj.__qualname__}</b>")
        parts.append("".join(lines).rstrip())
    source = "\n\n\n".join(parts)
    html = (
        f'<div style="font:12px Segoe UI,sans-serif;color:{vs.INK_SUBTLE};margin:0 0 4px">{" &middot; ".join(places)}</div>'
        f'<div style="background:{vs.RAISED};border:1px solid {vs.BORDER};border-radius:8px;padding:2px 12px;'
        f'overflow-x:auto;font-size:12px">{highlight(source, PythonLexer(), _CODE_STYLE)}</div>'
    )
    display({"text/html": html, "text/plain": source}, raw=True)


def table(frame, formats=None, caption=None, index=False):
    """Display a table with readable number formats, text and dates aligned left, and no row numbers."""
    formats = dict(formats or {})
    for column in frame.columns:
        if pd.api.types.is_datetime64_any_dtype(frame[column]):
            formats.setdefault(column, lambda d: f"{d:%a %b} {d.day}")
    styler = frame.style.format(formats, na_rep="", precision=3, thousands=",")
    text = [i for i, c in enumerate(frame.columns) if not pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(frame[c])]
    styler = styler.set_table_styles(
        [{"selector": f"td.col{i}, th.col_heading.col{i}", "props": "text-align:left"} for i in text], overwrite=False)
    if not index:
        styler = styler.hide(axis="index")
    if caption:
        styler = styler.set_caption(caption).set_table_styles(
            [{"selector": "caption", "props": f"caption-side:top;text-align:left;font-weight:600;color:{vs.INK};padding:4px 0"}],
            overwrite=False,
        )
    display(styler)


def multi_header(fig, axes, title, handles=(), labels=(), panel_titles=()):
    """Title and key above a grid of panels, plus a small title on each panel (a multi-panel vs.header)."""
    axes = list(np.ravel(axes))
    for ax, name in zip(axes, panel_titles):
        ax.set_title(name, loc="left", fontsize=vs.LABEL_SIZE, fontweight="semibold", color=vs.INK_MUTED, pad=6)
    first = axes[0]
    left = first.yaxis.get_tightbbox(fig.canvas.get_renderer()).x0
    x = first.transAxes.inverted().transform((left, 0))[0]
    lift = (vs.LABEL_SIZE * 1.4 + 10) if panel_titles else 4
    if handles:
        first.legend([vs._key(h) for h in handles], labels, loc="lower left", ncol=len(handles), bbox_to_anchor=(x, 1.0),
                     bbox_transform=offset_copy(first.transAxes, fig, y=lift, units="points"))
        lift += vs.LABEL_SIZE * 1.4 + 6
    first.text(x, 1.0, title, transform=offset_copy(first.transAxes, fig, y=lift, units="points"),
               fontsize=vs.TITLE_SIZE, fontweight="semibold", color=vs.INK, ha="left", va="bottom")


def money(x):
    return f"${x:,.0f}"

def git(*args):
    try:
        return subprocess.run(["git", *args], cwd=ROOT, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=30).stdout.rstrip()
    except (OSError, subprocess.SubprocessError):
        return "(git not available)"

The grain. Every fact table has one row per warehouse x department x day x shift. The planning grid adds a scenario. Three warehouses (1 is medium, 2 and 4 are large; there is no 3), three departments and three shifts.

rates = pd.read_csv(CSV_DIR / "comp_LaborCostAssumption.csv")
costed = history.merge(rates[["store_id", "dept_id", "loaded_regular_hourly_cost", "loaded_overtime_hourly_cost"]],
                       on=["store_id", "dept_id"], validate="many_to_one")
cost_error = (costed["labor_cost"] - costed["worked_regular_hours"] * costed["loaded_regular_hourly_cost"]
              - costed["worked_overtime_hours"] * costed["loaded_overtime_hourly_cost"]).abs().max()
day_sums = history.groupby(["store_id", "dept_id", "day_date"]).agg(shifts=("shift_demand_units", "sum"), day=("daily_demand_units", "first"))
history_daily = history.drop_duplicates(["store_id", "dept_id", "day_date"]).assign(
    week=lambda f: (f["day_date"] - pd.Timestamp("2026-01-01")).dt.days // 7 + 1)
same_weekday = (history_daily[history_daily["week"].between(3, 6)]
                .groupby(["store_id", "dept_id", "day_name"])["daily_demand_units"].mean())
bench_gap = (benchmark.set_index(["store_id", "dept_id", "day_name"])["predicted_transaction_count_proxy"]
             - same_weekday.reindex(benchmark.set_index(["store_id", "dept_id", "day_name"]).index)).abs().max()
template_keys, grid_keys = set(map(tuple, template[PLAN_KEY].values.tolist())), set(map(tuple, grid[PLAN_KEY].values.tolist()))
draft_match = template.merge(grid[[*PLAN_KEY, "draft_scheduled_employees"]], on=PLAN_KEY, suffixes=("", "_grid"))
closed_history = history[history["is_open"] == 0]
checks = pd.DataFrame(
    [
        ("Template keys equal the grid's keys", f"{len(template_keys & grid_keys)} shared, {len(template_keys ^ grid_keys)} unmatched",
         template_keys == grid_keys),
        ("Template draft values equal the grid's", f"{int((draft_match['draft_scheduled_employees'] != draft_match['draft_scheduled_employees_grid']).sum())} differ",
         bool((draft_match["draft_scheduled_employees"] == draft_match["draft_scheduled_employees_grid"]).all())),
        ("labor_cost = regular hours x regular rate + overtime hours x overtime rate", f"largest error {cost_error:.6f}", cost_error < 1e-6),
        ("Shift demand sums to the day's demand", f"largest gap {(day_sums['shifts'] - day_sums['day']).abs().max():.6f}",
         (day_sums["shifts"] - day_sums["day"]).abs().max() < 1e-6),
        ("Benchmark = mean of the same weekday in weeks 3-6", f"largest gap {bench_gap:.6f} over {len(benchmark)} rows", bench_gap < 1e-3),
        ("Closed history blocks have zero demand and no metric", f"{len(closed_history)} closed, "
         f"{int((closed_history['shift_demand_units'] != 0).sum())} with demand, {int(closed_history['metric_value'].notna().sum())} with a metric",
         bool((closed_history["shift_demand_units"] == 0).all() and closed_history["metric_value"].isna().all())),
    ],
    columns=["Check", "Result", "Pass"],
)

Closed blocks. History is closed on New Year's Day, and Pharmacy is closed on Saturday and Sunday evenings and Sunday mornings. The same Pharmacy blocks are closed in the planning week, so the template needs a 0 there. Closed blocks are left out of every fit (F-14, F-35).

Takeaway: the data is consistent with its own documents. Keys line up across the views, costs and demand add up exactly, and the benchmark is the simple average the docs describe. Everything below works at the block grain, and closed blocks get 0 and stay out of every model.

2. Diagnosis¶

What this shows: how service responds to how busy a block is, why worked staff matter more than scheduled staff, where history was over- and under-staffed, how often people call out, and how the current draft schedule would hold up in the planning week. (F-03, F-04, F-39, F-43, F-09, F-42)

Utilization is workload hours (demand x the department's labor standard) over hours actually worked. Each department has its own service metric and target (checkout wait, replenishment time, prescription wait), so we always compare the metric with its own target.

    blocks["utilization"], [0, 0.85, 0.90, np.inf], right=False, labels=["Below 0.85", "0.85 to 0.90", "0.90 and above"]))
cliff = named.pivot_table(index="band", columns="department", values="met_target", aggfunc="mean", observed=True)[list(DEPT.values())]
cliff["Blocks"] = named.groupby("band", observed=True).size()
cliff.loc["All blocks"] = [*named.groupby("department")["met_target"].mean()[list(DEPT.values())], len(named)]
table(cliff.reset_index().rename(columns={"band": "Utilization"}),
      {name: "{:.1%}" for name in DEPT.values()} | {"Blocks": "{:,.0f}"}, caption="Share of history blocks meeting target")

Worked, not scheduled. People call out, about half are replaced with overtime, and service follows the staff who actually worked. A block that lost someone met target less often than one that didn't.

Over and under. To locate the gaps, each block's need is the whole number of people that would have run it at 0.85 utilization, never below minimum staff (the starter queries' level, F-17). Hours above that are over, hours below are short.

Takeaway: service has a cliff, not a slope. Blocks are safe below 0.85 utilization, a coin flip from 0.85 to 0.90 and almost always miss above that, in every department. History had about the right number of hours in total, but in the wrong places: schedules follow habit while demand moves, and callouts take out people the schedule counted on. The draft rolls those habits forward, so many of its holiday-weekend blocks would run past the cliff, and in DISRUPT it schedules people who aren't available.

3. Forecast¶

What this shows: how the BASE demand forecast for each planning block is built and tested. The daily table, how holiday labels are matched across periods, the demand drivers we tested, the regression itself, its holiday effects against the data pack's own build script, a backtest against the benchmark, tests of borrowing a holiday effect and of splitting days into shifts, and the planning-week forecast. (F-41, F-44, F-45, F-61)

The planning grid has no demand, so it has to be forecast. We forecast each warehouse and department's daily demand, then split the day into shifts.

def fit_daily(train: pd.DataFrame):
    """Fit the regression on open days only (F-14)."""
    return smf.ols(FORMULA, train).fit()


def predict_daily(model, frame: pd.DataFrame, weeks) -> np.ndarray:
    """Forecast at the average weekly level of `weeks`, since the level of a future week isn't known."""
    return np.exp(np.mean([model.predict(frame.assign(week=week)) for week in weeks], axis=0))

src/forecast.py line 84: forecast_blocks
def forecast_blocks(valentine: dict[int, float] | None = None) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """BASE demand for every open planning block: daily forecast x shift share."""
    blocks = open_history()
    daily = forecast_daily(valentine, blocks)
    grid = load_planning_grid()
    open_grid = grid[(grid["scenario_code"] == "BASE") & (grid["is_open"] == 1)][BLOCK_KEY]
    frame = open_grid.merge(daily, on=["store_id", "dept_id", "day_date"], validate="many_to_one")
    frame = attach_shares(frame, shift_shares(blocks))
    totals = frame.groupby(["store_id", "dept_id", "day_date"])["share"].transform("sum")
    frame["share"] = frame["share"] / totals  # Keeps shifts summing to the day where a department closes some blocks.
    frame["base_demand"] = frame["daily_forecast"] * frame["share"]
    return frame

Takeaway: demand is almost entirely warehouse, weekday, holiday window and weekly level. Temperature and promotions add nothing once those are known, and traffic would leak the answer, so none of them is in the model. The regression recovers the build script's holiday effects and beats the benchmark on held-out weeks, but that edge comes from days the benchmark's averages distorted with holidays. In the planning week the two differ mainly on the holiday weekend, whose effect is borrowed from MLK, so the risk model carries extra uncertainty there.

4. Service curves¶

What this shows: the fitted link between utilization and each department's service metric, the data behind it, the utilization limits it implies, and how well its predicted chances match what happened out of sample. (F-46, F-62 to F-64, V-04, D-29)

The curve is fitted on log(metric / target), so 0 is exactly on target and every block's measured wait counts, not only whether it passed. That matters because few blocks sit near the cliff. Per department, the curve rises gently, bends smoothly upward and flattens at a cap, and each warehouse has its own level. The normal scatter around the curve turns a utilization into a chance of meeting target.

In [25]:
from src import service as sv

show_code(sv._bend, sv._curve, sv.Curve, sv.fit_curve)
src/service.py line 36: _bend · src/service.py line 41: _curve · src/service.py line 47: Curve · src/service.py line 70: fit_curve
def _bend(u, knot, width):
    """Softplus of u - knot: near 0 well below the knot, near u - knot well above it."""
    return width * np.logaddexp(0.0, (u - knot) / width)


def _curve(x, level1, level2, level4, slope, extra_slope, knot, cap, width):
    u, store_index = x
    levels = np.array([level1, level2, level4])[store_index.astype(int)]
    return np.minimum(cap, levels + slope * u + extra_slope * _bend(u, knot, width))


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Curve:
    levels: dict[int, float]
    slope: float
    extra_slope: float
    knot: float
    cap: float
    scatter: float
    width: float

    def log_ratio(self, store: int, u):
        u = np.asarray(u, dtype=float)
        return np.minimum(self.cap, self.levels[store] + self.slope * u + self.extra_slope * _bend(u, self.knot, self.width))

    def p_met(self, store: int, u):
        """Chance a block at utilization u meets its target."""
        return norm.cdf(-self.log_ratio(store, u) / self.scatter)

    def utilization_for(self, store: int, chance: float) -> float:
        """Utilization at which the chance of meeting target equals `chance`."""
        return float(brentq(lambda u: float(self.p_met(store, u)) - chance, 0.3, 1.2))


def fit_curve(blocks: pd.DataFrame) -> Curve:
    """Fit one department's curve. Tries several starting knots and widths, because the fit is sensitive to its start."""
    u = blocks["utilization"].to_numpy()
    y = np.log(blocks["service_ratio"].to_numpy())
    store_index = blocks["store_id"].map({s: i for i, s in enumerate(STORES)}).to_numpy()
    best, best_sse = None, np.inf
    for start_knot in (0.82, 0.85, 0.88, 0.90):
        for start_width in (0.01, 0.03):
            try:
                params, _ = curve_fit(
                    _curve,
                    (u, store_index),
                    y,
                    p0=[-4.0, -4.0, -4.0, 4.0, 10.0, start_knot, 1.45, start_width],
                    bounds=([-12, -12, -12, 0, 0, 0.70, 0.8, 0.003], [2, 2, 2, 12, 40, 0.97, 2.5, 0.15]),
                    maxfev=20000,
                )
            except RuntimeError:
                continue
            sse = float(((y - _curve((u, store_index), *params)) ** 2).sum())
            if sse < best_sse:
                best, best_sse = params, sse
    if best is None:
        raise RuntimeError("The service curve did not converge")
    level1, level2, level4, slope, extra_slope, knot, cap, width = best
    residuals = y - _curve((u, store_index), *best)
    in_range = (u >= SCATTER_RANGE[0]) & (u <= SCATTER_RANGE[1])
    return Curve({1: level1, 2: level2, 4: level4}, slope, extra_slope, knot, cap, float(residuals[in_range].std()), width)

Takeaway: one smooth curve per department reproduces the cliff, and the utilization that keeps a 95% chance sits just below it, with small differences between warehouses. Out of sample the curve's chances are far better than a flat rate, and they track observed rates near the goal. The first version, with a sharp kink, ran optimistic there, mostly in Front End, which is why we moved to the smooth bend (F-62 to F-64, D-29). The remaining assumption is that history's curve holds in the planning week (A-09).

5. Risk model¶

What this shows: how a block's chance of meeting target is calculated at any headcount. Three things can push a block over the cliff: demand above forecast, callouts that aren't backfilled, and the scatter around the service curve. The exact calculation is checked against a direct simulation of the same model. (F-47, D-07, D-18)

First, the inputs every planning block needs: demand (BASE forecast x the scenario's multiplier), its uncertainty, and a callout rate for its situation.

def planning_inputs(valentine: dict[int, float] | None = None) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """The planning grid with everything the search needs per open block: demand, uncertainty and callout rate."""
    grid = load_planning_grid()
    forecast = forecast_blocks(valentine)[["store_id", "dept_id", "day_date", "shift_code", "base_demand", "daily_forecast", "share"]]
    grid = grid.merge(forecast, on=["store_id", "dept_id", "day_date", "shift_code"], how="left", validate="many_to_one")
    grid["demand"] = grid["base_demand"] * grid["demand_multiplier"]
    grid["standard"] = grid["dept_id"].map(load_labor_standard())

    sd = forecast_sd().set_index("dept_id")["sd"]
    holiday_sd = grid["dept_id"].map(HOLIDAY_FACTOR_SD).where(grid["day_date"].isin(HOLIDAY_DATES), 0.0)
    grid["demand_sd"] = np.sqrt(grid["dept_id"].map(sd) ** 2 + holiday_sd**2)

    rates = callout_rates().set_index(["dept_id", "context"])["rate"]
    context = callout_context(grid)
    context = context.where(grid["day_date"] != DAY_AFTER_PRESIDENTS_DAY, "day_after_holiday")
    illness = grid["availability_note"].fillna("").str.contains(ILLNESS_NOTE)
    context = context.where(~illness, "flu_cluster")  # A-12: the DISRUPT illness cluster behaves like January's flu week.
    grid["callout_context"] = context
    grid["callout_rate"] = [rates[(dept, ctx)] for dept, ctx in zip(grid["dept_id"], context)]
    return grid

src/risk.py line 24: net_loss_distribution · src/risk.py line 39: chance_met
@lru_cache(maxsize=200_000)
def net_loss_distribution(employees: int, callout_rate: float, overtime_room: int, backfill: float = BACKFILL_SHARE):
    """Distribution of staff lost after backfill. Backfills can't exceed the overtime still free in the block."""
    most_callouts = int(binom.isf(1e-6, employees, callout_rate)) + 1 if employees else 0
    most_callouts = min(most_callouts, employees)
    pmf = np.zeros(most_callouts + 1)
    callout_pmf = binom.pmf(np.arange(most_callouts + 1), employees, callout_rate)
    for callouts in range(most_callouts + 1):
        backfills = np.arange(callouts + 1)
        backfill_pmf = binom.pmf(backfills, callouts, backfill)
        lost = callouts - np.minimum(backfills, overtime_room)
        np.add.at(pmf, lost, callout_pmf[callouts] * backfill_pmf)
    return pmf / pmf.sum()


def chance_met(
    curve: Curve,
    store: int,
    demand: float,
    demand_sd: float,
    employees: int,
    paid_hours: float,
    standard: float,
    callout_rate: float,
    overtime_room: int,
) -> float:
    """Chance this block meets its service target at this headcount."""
    if employees <= 0:
        return 0.0
    pmf = net_loss_distribution(int(employees), float(callout_rate), int(max(overtime_room, 0)))
    lost = np.arange(len(pmf))
    worked = np.maximum(employees - lost, 0)
    usable = worked > 0
    realized_demand = demand * np.exp(demand_sd * _NODES)
    utilization = np.outer(realized_demand * standard, 1.0 / (worked[usable] * paid_hours))
    by_outcome = (_WEIGHTS @ curve.p_met(store, utilization))
    return float(pmf[usable] @ by_outcome)

One block, three levels of risk. BASE, Warehouse 2 Front End, Saturday Feb 14, midday: a busy holiday-weekend block. The chance of meeting target at each headcount, with only the curve's scatter, then adding forecast error, then adding callouts (the full model). Dots are a 200,000-draw simulation of the full model at each headcount.

Takeaway: allowing for forecast error and callouts moves the headcount a block needs up by a few people, and that allowance is what keeps the plan off the cliff on an ordinary bad day. The exact calculation agrees with the simulation to within simulation noise, so the search can use the fast, repeatable exact version.

6. Allocation and cost¶

What this shows: how a block's total headcount is filled and costed, a worked example, and an independent recomputation of the costs straight from the README's wording. (V-08, R-25, A-01, A-10)

The README's rule: fill each block with available regular staff first, then with cross-trained staff from the partner department (Front End and Merchandising only), "limited to people that department is not already using in the same shift", then with overtime. How many are "not already used" isn't defined, so our reading is an assumption (A-01): the partner's regular staff left over after it fills its own total. Borrowed staff cost the regular rate of the block they cover (A-10). apply_rule() joins each block to its partner in the same shift and applies these three functions.

In [37]:
from src import allocation as al

show_code(al.usable_flex, al.allocate, al.block_cost)
src/allocation.py line 19: usable_flex · src/allocation.py line 25: allocate · src/allocation.py line 36: block_cost
def usable_flex(flex, partner_regular, partner_submitted):
    """Cross-trained staff this block can actually borrow (A-01)."""
    spare = np.maximum(0, np.asarray(partner_regular) - np.asarray(partner_submitted))
    return np.minimum(np.asarray(flex), spare)


def allocate(submitted, regular, overtime, usable):
    """Split totals into regular, flex and overtime. Anything left over can't be fielded."""
    submitted = np.asarray(submitted)
    filled_regular = np.minimum(submitted, regular)
    remaining = submitted - filled_regular
    filled_flex = np.minimum(remaining, usable)
    remaining = remaining - filled_flex
    filled_overtime = np.minimum(remaining, overtime)
    return filled_regular, filled_flex, filled_overtime, remaining - filled_overtime


def block_cost(regular, flex, overtime, paid_hours, regular_rate, overtime_rate):
    """Flex staff cost the regular rate of the block they cover (A-10)."""
    return (np.asarray(regular) + flex) * paid_hours * regular_rate + np.asarray(overtime) * paid_hours * overtime_rate

def readme_rule(frame, column):
    """The README's fill order and docs/ASSUMPTIONS.md section 5's cost formula, one row at a time."""
    rate = {(r.store_id, r.dept_id): (r.loaded_regular_hourly_cost, r.loaded_overtime_hourly_cost) for r in rates.itertuples()}
    rows = {(r.scenario_id, r.store_id, r.dept_id, r.day_date, r.shift_code): r for r in frame.itertuples()}
    partner_of = {38: 92, 92: 38}
    out = []
    for r in frame.itertuples():
        total, regular, overtime = int(getattr(r, column)), int(r.available_regular_employees), int(r.max_overtime_employees)
        usable = 0
        partner = rows.get((r.scenario_id, r.store_id, partner_of.get(r.dept_id), r.day_date, r.shift_code))
        if partner is not None:
            partner_using = min(int(getattr(partner, column)), int(partner.available_regular_employees))
            usable = min(int(r.cross_trained_flex_employees), int(partner.available_regular_employees) - partner_using)
        fill_regular = min(total, regular)
        fill_flex = min(total - fill_regular, usable)
        fill_overtime = min(total - fill_regular - fill_flex, overtime)
        regular_rate, overtime_rate = rate[(r.store_id, r.dept_id)]
        out.append({"i_capacity": regular + usable + overtime, "i_usable_flex": usable, "i_fill_regular": fill_regular, "i_fill_flex": fill_flex,
                    "i_fill_overtime": fill_overtime, "i_unfilled": total - fill_regular - fill_flex - fill_overtime,
                    "i_cost": (fill_regular + fill_flex) * r.paid_hours * regular_rate + fill_overtime * r.paid_hours * overtime_rate})
    return pd.concat([frame[[*PLAN_KEY, "scenario_code", "is_open", "paid_hours", column]].reset_index(drop=True), pd.DataFrame(out)], axis=1)


def check_costs(engine, column):
    """Compare the engine's allocation and cost with the independent rebuild, block by block and by scenario."""
    both = readme_rule(engine, column).merge(engine[[*PLAN_KEY, "capacity", "usable_flex", "fill_regular", "fill_flex", "fill_overtime", "unfilled", "cost"]],
                                             on=PLAN_KEY, validate="one_to_one")
    worst = {name: float((both["i_" + name] - both[name]).abs().max())
             for name in ["capacity", "usable_flex", "fill_regular", "fill_flex", "fill_overtime", "unfilled", "cost"]}
    opened = both[both["is_open"] == 1]
    totals = opened.groupby("scenario_code", sort=False)[["cost", "i_cost"]].sum().reindex(SCENARIOS)
    totals["gap"] = totals["i_cost"] - totals["cost"]
    return both, worst, totals


draft_check, worst, totals = check_costs(draft_ruled, "draft_scheduled_employees")

extra = (unfieldable["i_unfilled"] * unfieldable["paid_hours"] * unfieldable["loaded_overtime_hourly_cost"]).sum()

      f"staff who can be fielded; paying those people at overtime would add {money(extra)} (the README doesn't say how to cost them).")
assert all(v < 1e-6 for v in worst.values()), "The engine and the README rebuild disagree"

Takeaway: the cost rule is simple and fully traceable, and two independent implementations agree on every block of the draft. The one open question is a matter of reading: what "not already using" means for cross-trained staff (A-01). The draft's DISRUPT cost covers only the people who can actually be fielded.

7. Staffing search¶

What this shows: the search that sets every block's headcount, one shift's search laid out as a grid, the plans for all three scenarios against the draft, where capacity runs out, an independent check that the search finds the best answer under its rule, and the reason attached to every block. (F-48, F-50, V-07, D-06, D-17)

Front End and Merchandising are searched together in each shift because they share cross-trained staff; Pharmacy is searched alone. No solver is needed: each shift has at most a few hundred feasible pairs, so the search tries them all and keeps the best by, in order, (1) the sum of the departments' chances of meeting target, each capped at the service goal (A-13); (2) the fewest hours short of need; (3) the lowest cost. A department only lends people it doesn't need itself (D-17).

src/search.py line 75: needed_employees · src/search.py line 89: solve_pair · src/search.py line 114: solve_single · src/search.py line 120: build_plan
def needed_employees(row, curves: dict[int, Curve], goal: float) -> int:
    """Smallest headcount reaching the goal, ignoring capacity."""
    limit = 3 * int(row.available_regular_employees + row.max_overtime_employees + row.cross_trained_flex_employees) + 20
    employees = int(row.min_staff)
    while employees < limit and _block_chance(row, employees, curves) < goal:
        employees += 1
    return employees


def solve_pair(front, merch, curves: dict[int, Curve], goal: float) -> tuple[int, int]:
    """Best feasible Front End and Merchandising headcounts for one shift."""
    front_n, front_p = _chances(front, curves)
    merch_n, merch_p = _chances(merch, curves)
    front_need = needed_employees(front, curves, goal)
    merch_need = needed_employees(merch, curves, goal)
    keep_front = front_n >= min(front_need, int(front.available_regular_employees + front.max_overtime_employees))
    keep_merch = merch_n >= min(merch_need, int(merch.available_regular_employees + merch.max_overtime_employees))
    front_n, front_p = front_n[keep_front], front_p[keep_front]
    merch_n, merch_p = merch_n[keep_merch], merch_p[keep_merch]
    f, m = np.meshgrid(front_n, merch_n, indexing="ij")
    front_usable = usable_flex(front.cross_trained_flex_employees, merch.available_regular_employees, m)
    merch_usable = usable_flex(merch.cross_trained_flex_employees, front.available_regular_employees, f)
    feasible = (f <= front.available_regular_employees + front.max_overtime_employees + front_usable) & (
        m <= merch.available_regular_employees + merch.max_overtime_employees + merch_usable
    )
    score = np.minimum(front_p, goal)[:, None] + np.minimum(merch_p, goal)[None, :]
    score = np.where(feasible, np.round(score, SCORE_DECIMALS), -np.inf)
    shortfall = np.maximum(0, front_need - f) * front.paid_hours + np.maximum(0, merch_need - m) * merch.paid_hours
    cost = _cost(f, front, front_usable) + _cost(m, merch, merch_usable)
    order = np.lexsort((cost.ravel(), shortfall.ravel(), -score.ravel()))
    i, j = np.unravel_index(order[0], f.shape)
    return int(f[i, j]), int(m[i, j])


def solve_single(row, curves: dict[int, Curve], goal: float) -> int:
    """Best feasible headcount for a department that doesn't share staff."""
    top = max(int(row.available_regular_employees + row.max_overtime_employees), int(row.min_staff))
    return min(needed_employees(row, curves, goal), top)


def build_plan(inputs: pd.DataFrame, curves: dict[int, Curve], goal: float = SERVICE_GOAL) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Recommended total employees for all 567 rows. Closed blocks are 0."""
    plan = inputs.copy()
    plan["recommended"] = 0
    open_rows = plan[plan["is_open"] == 1]
    for _, shift in open_rows.groupby(["scenario_id", "store_id", "day_date", "shift_code"], sort=False):
        by_dept = {row.dept_id: row for row in shift.itertuples()}
        if 95 in by_dept:
            plan.loc[by_dept[95].Index, "recommended"] = solve_single(by_dept[95], curves, goal)
        if 38 in by_dept and 92 in by_dept:
            front, merch = solve_pair(by_dept[38], by_dept[92], curves, goal)
            plan.loc[by_dept[38].Index, "recommended"] = front
            plan.loc[by_dept[92].Index, "recommended"] = merch
        else:
            for dept in (38, 92):
                if dept in by_dept:
                    plan.loc[by_dept[dept].Index, "recommended"] = solve_single(by_dept[dept], curves, goal)
    return plan

Is each pick the best one? An independent brute force over every pair in every open shift, written from the rule as stated at the top of this section. It scores headcounts with the fitted curves and chance_met() only, and doesn't call the search or the allocation code. (V-07)

def b_chance(b, n):
    room = int(b.max_overtime_employees) - max(0, n - int(b.available_regular_employees))
    return rk.chance_met(curves[b.dept_id], b.store_id, b.demand, b.demand_sd, n, b.paid_hours, b.standard, b.callout_rate, room)


def b_need(b):
    limit, n = 3 * int(b.available_regular_employees + b.max_overtime_employees + b.cross_trained_flex_employees) + 20, int(b.min_staff)
    while n < limit and b_chance(b, n) < goal:
        n += 1
    return n


def b_cost(b, n, usable):
    regular = min(n, int(b.available_regular_employees))
    flex = min(n - regular, usable)
    overtime = min(n - regular - flex, int(b.max_overtime_employees))
    return (regular + flex) * b.paid_hours * b.loaded_regular_hourly_cost + overtime * b.paid_hours * b.loaded_overtime_hourly_cost


def brute_pair(fe, me):
    """Every (Front End, Merchandising) pair; returns the best with and without the D-17 floors, ties and pair count."""
    own = lambda b: int(b.available_regular_employees + b.max_overtime_employees)
    span = lambda b: range(int(b.min_staff), max(own(b) + int(b.cross_trained_flex_employees), int(b.min_staff)) + 1)
    pf, pm = {n: b_chance(fe, n) for n in span(fe)}, {n: b_chance(me, n) for n in span(me)}
    need_f, need_m = b_need(fe), b_need(me)
    rows = []
    for f, p_f in pf.items():
        for m, p_m in pm.items():
            usable_f = min(int(fe.cross_trained_flex_employees), max(0, int(me.available_regular_employees) - m))
            usable_m = min(int(me.cross_trained_flex_employees), max(0, int(fe.available_regular_employees) - f))
            if f > own(fe) + usable_f or m > own(me) + usable_m:
                continue
            rows.append((-round(min(p_f, goal) + min(p_m, goal), 3), max(0, need_f - f) * fe.paid_hours + max(0, need_m - m) * me.paid_hours,
                         b_cost(fe, f, usable_f) + b_cost(me, m, usable_m), f, m, f >= min(need_f, own(fe)) and m >= min(need_m, own(me))))
    guarded = [r for r in rows if r[5]]
    best, unguarded = min(guarded, key=lambda r: r[:3]), min(rows, key=lambda r: r[:3])
    ties = sum(r[:2] == best[:2] and abs(r[2] - best[2]) < 1e-9 for r in guarded)
    return (best[3], best[4]), (unguarded[3], unguarded[4]), ties, len(rows)


def brute_single(b):
    need, top = b_need(b), max(int(b.available_regular_employees + b.max_overtime_employees), int(b.min_staff))
    return min((-round(min(b_chance(b, n), goal), 3), max(0, need - n) * b.paid_hours, b_cost(b, n, 0), n) for n in range(int(b.min_staff), top + 1))[3]

def why_text(row, need: int, goal: float) -> str:
    """The main reason for the recommendation."""
    change = row.recommended - row.draft_scheduled_employees
    draft_clause = f"The draft's {row.draft_scheduled_employees} people would run at {_percent(row.planned_utilization_draft)} utilization, with {_a_percent(row.chance_met_draft)} chance of meeting target."
    if row.unfilled_draft > 0:
        draft_clause = (
            f"The draft schedules {row.draft_scheduled_employees} people, but only {row.fielded_draft} can be fielded. They would run at "
            f"{_percent(row.planned_utilization_draft)} utilization, with {_a_percent(row.chance_met_draft)} chance of meeting target."
        )
    if row.chance_met < goal - 0.0005:
        return (
            f"This block can't reach the goal. It needs {need} people for a {_percent(goal)} chance of meeting target, but the plan can only field "
            f"{row.recommended}, using all of its own regular staff and overtime. {draft_clause} The plan's chance is {_short_percent(row.chance_met, goal)}."
        )
    if change > 0:
        return f"{draft_clause} Adding {change} brings it to {_percent(row.planned_utilization)} utilization and {_a_percent(row.chance_met)} chance."
    if change < 0:
        return f"{draft_clause} That is more than this block needs. With {row.recommended}, it runs at {_percent(row.planned_utilization)} utilization and still has {_a_percent(row.chance_met)} chance."
    return f"{draft_clause} That already reaches the {_percent(goal)} goal, so there is no change."
BASE example Block Headline Why
Largest addition Warehouse 2, Sun Feb 15, Front End, Midday Add 15: 32 in the draft to 47 in the plan The draft's 32 people would run at 108% utilization, with a 0% chance of meeting target. Adding 15 brings it to 73% utilization and a 97% chance.
Largest cut Warehouse 4, Wed Feb 18, Merchandising, Opening Cut 3: 21 in the draft to 18 in the plan The draft's 21 people would run at 64% utilization, with a 100% chance of meeting target. That is more than this block needs. With 18, it runs at 75% utilization and still has a 98% chance.
Lowest chance Warehouse 1, Sat Feb 14, Front End, Midday Add 5: 29 in the draft to 34 in the plan This block can't reach the goal. It needs 39 people for a 95% chance of meeting target, but the plan can only field 34, using all of its own regular staff and overtime. The draft's 29 people would run at 96% utilization, with a 5% chance of meeting target. The plan's chance is 57%.

Takeaway: moving and adding hours lifts expected service sharply in every scenario for a moderate rise in cost, and no block is above capacity. What no schedule can fix is capacity itself: the blocks still below the goal already use all their own regular staff and overtime, and they cluster on the holiday weekend. Two independent rebuilds confirm the costs and that every pick is the best one under the stated rule.

def pto_what_if(inputs: pd.DataFrame, curves: dict[int, Curve], goal: float = SERVICE_GOAL, limits=(0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5)) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Keep up to N more people per block by limiting PTO in BASE, never more than the block lost to PTO."""
    base = inputs[inputs["scenario_code"] == "BASE"]
    drop = np.floor(pto_drop(base) + 0.5)
    rows = []
    for limit in limits:
        recovered = drop.clip(upper=limit).astype(int)
        trial = base.copy()
        trial["available_regular_employees"] = trial["available_regular_employees"] + recovered
        result = evaluate(build_plan(trial, curves, goal), "recommended", curves)
        summary = summarize(result, goal).iloc[0]
        short = result[(result["is_open"] == 1) & (result["chance_met"] < goal - 0.0005)]
        rows.append(
            {
                "kept_per_block": limit,
                "people_kept": int(recovered.sum()),
                "blocks_below_goal": int(summary["below_goal"]),
                "below_goal_with_holiday_pto": int(short["availability_note"].eq(PTO_NOTE).sum()),
                "expected_met": float(summary["expected_met"]),
                "cost": float(summary["cost"]),
                "overtime_hours": float(summary["overtime_hours"]),
            }
        )
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

def valentine_sensitivity(curves: dict, plan_row: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """T-22: what if the true Valentine's uplift differs from the one the plan assumes?

    The BASE plan stays fixed, and only Feb 14 blocks are scored against each possible uplift.
    Also shows what planning for that uplift would have cost.
    """
    rows = []
    for uplift in VALENTINE_CASES:
        values = {38: uplift, 92: uplift, 95: 0.0}
        inputs = planning_inputs(values)
        fixed = inputs.copy()
        fixed["recommended"] = plan_row["recommended"].to_numpy()
        scored = evaluate(fixed, "recommended", curves)
        replanned = evaluate(build_plan(inputs, curves), "recommended", curves)
        pick = lambda frame: frame[
            (frame["scenario_code"] == "BASE") & (frame["is_open"] == 1) & (frame["day_date"] == "2026-02-14") & (frame["dept_id"] != 95)
        ]
        rows.append(
            {
                "true_uplift": uplift,
                "our_plan_expected_met": pick(scored)["chance_met"].mean(),
                "replanned_expected_met": pick(replanned)["chance_met"].mean(),
                "replanned_feb14_cost": pick(replanned)["cost"].sum(),
                "our_plan_feb14_cost": pick(scored)["cost"].sum(),
            }
        )
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

Takeaway: each extra point of expected service costs more than the last, and the 95% goal sits before the steepest part of the curve. The extra cost over the draft is the price of allowing for forecast error and callouts; moving hours alone, at about the draft's cost, already beats the draft under every assumption about how judging treats callouts. Limiting holiday PTO is the strongest single lever: fewer blocks miss the goal, and cost falls as regular staff replace overtime. The Valentine's uplift barely matters, because most of those blocks are at capacity either way.

PEAK changes only demand, concentrated on the holiday weekend, so its plan adds hours there, and it ends with the lowest expected service because the surge lands on days that are already at capacity. In every scenario the plan gains most on the holiday weekend, where the draft is weakest.

def fill_template(plan: pd.DataFrame, column: str = "recommended", team_id: str = TEAM_ID) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Fill the template by joining on keys, keeping its row order and columns (F-15)."""
    template = pd.read_csv(TEMPLATE_PATH, parse_dates=["day_date"])
    values = plan[[*PLAN_KEY, column]].rename(columns={column: "_value"})
    filled = template.merge(values, on=PLAN_KEY, how="left", validate="one_to_one")
    filled["submitted_employees"] = filled["_value"]
    filled["team_id"] = team_id
    return filled[TEMPLATE_COLUMNS]

11. Reproducibility¶

What this shows: whether this notebook's own recalculation reproduces the results we submitted. Every entry of outputs/analysis_summary.json, the file the report reads its figures from, is rebuilt from the objects computed above, with the same rounding the pipeline uses, and compared value by value. Then the main result files in outputs/ are compared block by block. Any difference stops the notebook with an error. (V-01, D-28)

def differences(mine, theirs, path=""):
    """Every (path, ours, saved) that differs; numbers within a relative 1e-9 count as equal."""
    if isinstance(theirs, dict) and isinstance(mine, dict):
        if set(mine) != set(theirs):
            yield path + " (keys)", sorted(set(mine) - set(theirs)), sorted(set(theirs) - set(mine))
        for key in set(mine) & set(theirs):
            yield from differences(mine[key], theirs[key], f"{path}.{key}")
    elif isinstance(theirs, list) and isinstance(mine, list):
        if len(mine) != len(theirs):
            yield path + " (length)", len(mine), len(theirs)
        for i, (a, b) in enumerate(zip(mine, theirs)):
            yield from differences(a, b, f"{path}[{i}]")
    elif isinstance(theirs, (int, float)) and isinstance(mine, (int, float, np.number)) and not isinstance(theirs, bool):
        if not (abs(float(mine) - theirs) <= 1e-9 * max(1.0, abs(theirs)) or (np.isnan(float(mine)) and np.isnan(theirs))):
            yield path, mine, theirs
    elif mine != theirs:
        yield path, mine, theirs


def count_values(value):
    if isinstance(value, dict):
        return sum(count_values(v) for v in value.values())
    if isinstance(value, list):
        return sum(count_values(v) for v in value)
    return 1

def read_csv_output(name, **kw):
    return pd.read_csv(io.BytesIO(read_output(name)), **kw)


def frame_gap(ours, theirs, keys, numbers=(), texts=()):
    """Largest relative gap in numbers and count of text mismatches, after joining on keys."""
    ours, theirs = ours.copy(), theirs.copy()
    for frame in (ours, theirs):
        for key in keys:
            if "date" in key:
                frame[key] = pd.to_datetime(frame[key])
    joined = ours.merge(theirs, on=keys, suffixes=("", "_saved"), how="outer", indicator=True, validate="one_to_one")
    unmatched = int((joined["_merge"] != "both").sum())
    gap = max([float(((joined[c] - joined[c + "_saved"]).abs() / joined[c + "_saved"].abs().clip(lower=1)).max()) for c in numbers] or [0.0])
    text_gap = sum(int((joined[c].fillna("") != joined[c + "_saved"].fillna("")).sum()) for c in texts)
    return len(joined), unmatched, gap, text_gap
